note: The CPython surfaces worth filling, ordered by how much of the corpus they
cost. Coverage is COMPUTED, not maintained here: `stdlib-plan` reads the
`# fills:` header of every committed unit and drops a target whose names are
all taken, so a fully covered target stays in this file on purpose. It
documents the surface, and it reopens by itself if a unit is ever removed or
if a fresh census widens what the surface means.
Every weight carries the command and the date that produced it (invariant 3).
Nothing in this file is re-counted by any tool; re-run the census to move a
number, and move its date with it.

columns.programs: corpus programs that reach for the module at all
columns.sightings: occurrences, so one program may count several times
columns.sole_gap: programs where this module is the SOLE reason the engine refused — the column that says what filling it would actually buy

note: These are counts of one corpus on one day, not a forecast of demand and not
a claim about any other population. Capture grows the corpus every session,
so a later scan will disagree; that is the corpus growing, not this file
being wrong. Re-run before relying on a number here.

closed_kinds_note: This list restates `lypning.engines.ONLY_CPYTHON_REFUSALS` so a reader sees
the reasons without holding two files open. `stdlib_generate.load_targets`
CHECKS it against the engine's own set and refuses to plan if the two differ:
a kind the engine added and this file did not name would become a target
nobody excluded, which is precisely the silent wrong answer the closed list
exists to prevent. Fix this file when they diverge — never the engine's set
(invariant 1: never widen a table to silence a mismatch).

why: A reimplementation here is wrong in a way the cases cannot catch. A
pure-Python `math.log` agrees with CPython on the twelve values a unit
prints and diverges in the last place on the thirteenth; a hand-rolled
JSON float repr agrees until it meets 0.1 + 0.2; `random` is a specific
MT19937 stream, not an arbitrary one. Every other unit in this corpus
fails LOUDLY when it is wrong, because CPython runs every case and a
wrong byte rejects the unit. These fail quietly, and a model that
reproduced one inline would ship a wrong answer wearing the shape of a
feature.
Observable order, object identity and type names are CPython's own, not a
computable property a helper can restore. A set-ordering helper agrees
under this machine's hash seed and under no other; a `glob` wrapper that
sorts is a different function than the one the program called.

never_target.reason: refused by design, not by omission
why: The heaviest surface in the census and still out of scope: see
docs/SUBSET.md section 5. Nothing in pure Python spawns a process, so a
'fill' could only be a stub that lies about what it did. A high count
here is a statement about what the corpus does, not a backlog item.

never_target.reason: refused by design, not by omission
why: `ast` is CPython's own parser exposed as data. A pure-Python Python parser
would be a second grammar to keep in step with the first, and the engine
refuses `ast` because it will not carry one either. A unit here would be
a large, plausible, quietly divergent parser — the worst shape a corpus
row can have.

never_target.reason: refused by design, not by omission
why: A clock is not a function of its arguments. Reading one makes a unit's
output differ between two runs, and the file format requires output that
is byte-identical on every run on every machine. The date ARITHMETIC that
surrounds a clock is a separate, fillable target and is listed below as
`datetime_datetime`; the clock read itself never is.

targets.fillable: the deterministic half only: how a candidate name is composed from prefix, the random infix and suffix, how `dir` defaults are chosen, and the `text`/binary mode flags — all as functions taking the infix as an argument.
targets.caution: tempfile's NAME GENERATION is `random`, a closed kind, and the path it returns is a temp path that may never appear in a unit's output. Fill the composition, take the random part as a parameter, and say in the docstring that the RNG half is deliberately absent. A unit that prints an actual temp path is rejected for non-determinism.

targets.fillable: the path and buffer arithmetic: how `which` splits PATH and applies PATHEXT, how `copyfileobj` chunks, how an archive member name is built from a base and a root.
targets.caution: everything in shutil that WALKS a directory needs `os.listdir`, which the engine refuses, and `os.environ`, which it also refuses. Take PATH and the directory listing as arguments; do not read them.

targets.fillable: all of it, as functions returning materialised lists.
targets.caution: CPython returns iterators and this unit cannot: `yield` is refused. Return lists, and say in the docstring that laziness and infinite inputs are the accepted divergence. `itertools.count`, `cycle` and `repeat` are unbounded and are deliberately not listed. `itertools.batched` is deliberately not listed either, and for a different reason: it arrived in CPython 3.12, and the oracle is whatever `python3` resolves to (`stdlib-verify --cpython`, default `the real python3, past any shim`) — 3.11.15 in this tree, checked 2026-09-17, where `itertools.batched` does not exist. `names` is an instruction the generate and repair prompts render verbatim as the names a unit must fill, so a name the oracle may not have is a helper the reference differential silently skips on one machine and checks on another.

targets.fillable: the ones that are exact arithmetic over the input.
targets.caution: `statistics.geometric_mean` needs exp/log and is NOT listed: `math` is a closed kind. Anything that would reach for a transcendental is out, and a unit that approximates one is exactly the quiet divergence the closed list forbids.

targets.fillable: all of it. SequenceMatcher becomes `matcher_new(a, b)` returning a dict plus `matching_blocks(st)`, `opcodes(st)` and `ratio(st)` — the dict-as-state idiom.
targets.caution: CPython's autojunk heuristic (the 1 percent popular-element rule for sequences of 200 or more) changes the answer and must either be implemented or declared absent in the docstring. `find_longest_match` recurses; carry an explicit stack, because depth beyond 180 frames is refused.

targets.fillable: a DECLARED, BOUNDED code-point range with its table written out in the file — U+0000..U+00FF is the useful one, and the cases must cover every code point in whatever range the docstring claims.
targets.caution: the full UCD is megabytes of tables and no unit carries it. The docstring must state the exact range covered and the helper must raise `ValueError("...")` outside it rather than guess, because a table that silently answers for an uncovered code point is a silent wrong answer. Do not attempt full NFC/NFD.

targets.fillable: the remaining parse entry points, on top of what the committed urllib units already cover.
targets.caution: kept in the file although the committed units may already cover every name: the plan drops it when they do, and reopens it if one is removed.

targets.fillable: the container format on bytes: the local file header, the central directory, the end-of-central-directory record, and STORED (method 0) members. Read and write, as functions over `bytes`.
targets.caution: DEFLATE is not fillable — it is zlib, and a from-scratch inflater in this subset would be large and quietly wrong on the cases it does not print. Handle method 0 and raise `ValueError("unsupported compression method")` for anything else. CRC-32 is already a committed unit; inline the same algorithm rather than importing anything.

targets.fillable: datetime-as-a-dict arithmetic on top of the committed date units: combining a date and a time, normalising a timedelta, fixed-offset timezones.
targets.caution: no clock. `datetime.now`, `today` and `utcnow` are never filled — every helper takes its instant as an argument. Leap seconds do not exist in CPython's model either; say so rather than inventing them.

targets.fillable: the binascii spelling of base64, which differs from the base64 module's: `b2a_base64` appends a newline unless `newline=False`, and `a2b_base64` is lenient about padding in a way `base64.b64decode` is not.
targets.caution: a committed unit already fills base64. The DIFFERENCE is the point of this one, and the docstring must name it; a unit that just re-does base64 under another name is a duplicate and will be dropped at assemble.

targets.fillable: all of it. The constants are literals; `Template.substitute` and `safe_substitute` become functions over the template string.
targets.caution: `string.Template` is a class and classes are refused — write `substitute(template, mapping)`. Its placeholder rule is `$$`, `$name` and `${name}` with an identifier that may not start with a digit, and `substitute` raises where `safe_substitute` does not; that difference is the unit.

targets.fillable: a parser as a dict: `parser_new(prog)`, `add_argument(st, ...)`, `parse_args(st, argv)` returning a dict rather than a Namespace. Long and short options, `store_true`, `nargs` counts, `--` and `=` forms, positionals, defaults and `type=int`.
targets.caution: the lowest weight here and listed last on purpose. argparse's error MESSAGES and its usage-line layout are large surfaces of their own; cover parsing, declare the messages out of scope in the docstring, and raise `ValueError("...")` where CPython would exit.
